mainTopic: The end of פרק הֶשֵּׂג יָד and the start of the next פרק: pledging one's weight or height to הקדש
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier discussion: the ברייתא should have used the Torah's words זכר and נקבה. The גמרא then asks why an elderly woman's ערך drops to exactly a third, while an elderly man's drops lower. חזקיה answers with a folk saying: an old man at home is a burden, but an old woman at home is a treasure. After the הדרן, a new משנה teaches that one who pledges 'my weight' pays his weight in silver or gold, whichever he named. The same משנה tells how ירמטיא's mother paid her daughter's weight in gold. It also records an argument between רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי about how to measure the weight of a hand. The גמרא learns that if no metal was named, any material sold by weight in that place counts, as רחבה and רב פפא explain. It then explains the story of ירמטיא's mother: an important person's vow is judged by his status. Finally, רב יהודה splits 'my height' from 'my full height' by following רבי עקיבא, who learns meaning from extra words, and a new question about 'עומדי' continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The wording should have been 'male and female'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא wraps up an earlier discussion: the ברייתא should have used the words זכר and נקבה, the Torah's own terms for ערכין.
steps.simpleTranslation: It should have said: 'that of a male and that of a female.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a discussion from just before this section. It says the ברייתא should have used the words 'male' and 'female.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah's section on ערכין uses the words זכר and נקבה. The words 'son' and 'daughter' belong to a different topic (יוצא דופן). So the correct wording for a ברייתא about ערכין is 'male and female.'

keyTerms.meaning: It should have said / it needed to say
Male (the Torah's word in the section on ערכין)
Female (the Torah's word in the section on ערכין)

steps.confusionAlert: This line does not start a new topic. It is the last line of a discussion that began before this section.

phrases.english: It should have said: 'that of a male and that of a female.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes a discussion about the wording of a ברייתא that began before this section.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: In ערכין the correct terms are זכר and נקבה.

steps.title: Why does an old woman keep a third of her value but an old man does not?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why a woman over sixty keeps exactly one third of her earlier ערך, while a man over sixty keeps less than a third.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is different about a female, that when she grows old she stands at one third? And what is different about a male, that he does not stand at one third?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question about the Torah's numbers for ערכין. This sets up חזקיה's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Between ages twenty and sixty, a woman's ערך is 30 שקלים, and after sixty it drops to 10, exactly one third. A man's ערך is 50 שקלים, and after sixty it drops to 15, which is less than a third. The גמרא wants to know why the man loses more.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different? (asks for the reason behind a distinction)
She grows old
She stands at / remains at
At one third

phrases.english: And what is different about a female,
that when she grows old she stands at one third,
phrases.notes: From 30 שקלים down to 10, exactly one third.

phrases.english: and what is different about a male,
that he does not stand at one third?
phrases.notes: From 50 שקלים down to 15, which is less than a third.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question about the ערכין values themselves.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason an elderly man's ערך drops by a larger proportion than an elderly woman's.

steps.title: An old man is a burden, an old woman is a treasure
steps.stepSummary: חזקיה answers with a popular saying: an old man in the house is a burden, while an old woman in the house is a treasure.
steps.simpleTranslation: חזקיה said: People say: An old man in the house is a burden in the house. An old woman in the house is a treasure in the house.
steps.whatsHappening: חזקיה answers the question by quoting a common folk saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An elderly man usually cannot do much work at home. An elderly woman can still help with many household tasks. Because she stays more useful, her value drops less.

keyTerms.meaning: People say (introduces a folk saying)
An old man / an old woman
A burden, something useless
A treasure

steps.whatToRemember: A woman's ערך drops less in old age because an elderly woman is still useful in the home, as the saying goes.

phrases.english: חזקיה said: People say:
An old man in the house is a burden in the house;
an old woman in the house is a treasure in the house.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: An elderly woman still contributes at home and an elderly man does not, so her value falls less.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing the chapter הֶשֵּׂג יָד
steps.stepSummary: The closing line of the chapter הֶשֵּׂג יָד.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, הֶשֵּׂג יָד.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the standard closing line of a chapter. The chapter הֶשֵּׂג יָד is now finished.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line marks the end of the chapter. Next comes a new משנה with a new topic.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you (the formula that closes a chapter)
'What one can afford', the name of the chapter just finished

phrases.english: We will return to you, הֶשֵּׂג יָד.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the chapter after the final discussion.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: End of the chapter הֶשֵּׂג יָד.

steps.title: Pledging 'my weight' to the Temple
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה rules that someone who says 'my weight is upon me' gives his weight in silver or gold, whichever he specified.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who says 'My weight is upon me' gives his weight. If he said silver, he gives silver; if he said gold, he gives gold.
steps.whatsHappening: A new chapter begins with a משנה. It teaches what someone owes after pledging his own weight.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A pledge of 'my weight' is different from a pledge of ערך, which has a fixed price set by the Torah. Here he must donate an amount equal to his body weight. If he named silver or gold, he gives that metal.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה (marks the start of a משנה)
'My weight is upon me', a pledge to donate one's weight
He gives his weight (in the material he named)
Silver / gold

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who says: 'My weight is upon me'
gives his weight,

phrases.aramaic: אִם כֶּסֶף כָּסֶף, וְאִם זָהָב זָהָב.
phrases.english: if silver, silver, and if gold, gold.
phrases.notes: He means: whatever metal he named in his pledge is the metal he gives.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new chapter and topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A pledge of 'my weight' requires donating one's body weight in the metal he specified.

steps.title: The story of ירמטיא's mother
steps.stepSummary: The משנה tells about the mother of ירמטיא, who pledged her daughter's weight and paid it in gold in ירושלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was an incident with the mother of ירמטיא, who said: 'My daughter's weight is upon me.' She went up to ירושלים and paid her daughter's weight in gold.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה backs up its rule with a real story. A mother pledged her daughter's weight and actually paid it in gold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story shows that the 'weight' pledge was really carried out. It also shows that one can pledge someone else's weight, not only one's own.

keyTerms.meaning: An incident, a story from real life
My daughter's weight
She went up to ירושלים

steps.whatToRemember: A pledge of weight is paid by weighing the person and giving that weight. ירמטיא's mother paid her daughter's weight in gold, even though she had not said 'gold.' The גמרא asks about this in step 19.

phrases.english: There was an incident with the mother of ירמטיא
who said: 'My daughter's weight is upon me,'
and she went up to ירושלים
and weighed her, paying her weight in gold.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the rule of step 5 with a real case.
steps.raayaObject: That a weight pledge is carried out by weighing the person and paying that weight.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of ירמטיא's mother paying her daughter's weight in gold.

steps.title: Pledging the weight of one's hand: the water-barrel method
steps.stepSummary: The משנה moves to someone who pledges the weight of his hand. רבי יהודה describes a method using water displacement and donkey meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says 'the weight of my hand is upon me,' רבי יהודה says: he fills a barrel with water, puts his arm in up to the elbow, then weighs out donkey meat, bones and sinews and puts them in until the barrel is full again.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings a new case: a person pledged only the weight of his hand. רבי יהודה gives a practical way to find out how much that hand weighs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You cannot cut off a hand to weigh it, so רבי יהודה measures it by the water it pushes out. Donkey meat, bone and sinew are put in to take the hand's place, since they are similar to a human arm. Then that material is weighed.

keyTerms.meaning: "The weight of my hand is upon me": a pledge to donate the weight of one's hand
Barrel
His elbow
Donkey meat
Sinews

phrases.english: "The weight of my hand is upon me,"
Rabbi Yehuda says:
He fills a barrel with water,
and puts it [his hand] in up to his elbow,
and he weighs out donkey meat, bones and sinews
and puts them into it until it is full.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's weight pledges, now for one body part instead of the whole body.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A pledge of a hand's weight is measured by water displacement, filling the space with donkey meat, bones and sinews and weighing them.

steps.title: רבי יוסי rejects the method and says to estimate
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי argues that donkey parts can never match human flesh and bone exactly. Instead we estimate how much the hand likely weighs.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי said: how can you possibly match flesh to flesh and bone to bone? Rather, we estimate how much the hand probably weighs.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי attacks רבי יהודה's method as impossible to get exact. He gives his own approach: just make an estimate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Donkey flesh and bone do not weigh exactly the same as the same amount of human flesh and bone, and you cannot match the right mix of each. So filling the same space with them won't give the true weight. רבי יוסי says an estimate is the best we can do.

keyTerms.meaning: "But how...?": a question that challenges the idea before it
To match exactly
We estimate the value or amount
How much it is likely to weigh

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei said:
But how is it possible to match
flesh against flesh
and bones against bones?
Rather, we estimate the hand:
how much it is likely to weigh.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי: וְכִי הֵיאַךְ אֶפְשָׁר לְכַוֵּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יהודה's method and offers a different one.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Donkey parts cannot exactly match human flesh and bone, so the method gives a wrong weight.

steps.title: What does 'if silver, silver; if gold, gold' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by asking what the משנה meant by 'if silver, silver; if gold, gold.'
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: What does 'if silver, silver; if gold, gold' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins and goes back to the first line of the משנה from step 5. It asks what that phrase means, and this sets up the explanation that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase could be read different ways. It could mean the person chooses, or that the type of pledge decides the metal. The גמרא wants it spelled out.

keyTerms.meaning: גמרא: marks where the discussion on the משנה begins
What? The גמרא is asking what something means

keyTerms.term: אִם כֶּסֶף כֶּסֶף אִם זָהָב זָהָב
keyTerms.meaning: "If silver, silver; if gold, gold": the משנה's phrase being explained

phrases.english: GEMARA:
What is "if silver, silver,
if gold, gold"?
phrases.notes: This is quoting the משנה's ruling from step 5 about someone who says 'my weight is upon me.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי ״אִם כֶּסֶף כֶּסֶף אִם זָהָב זָהָב״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back from the end of the משנה to its opening ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the משנה's phrase 'if silver, silver; if gold, gold' means.

steps.title: It depends on what he specified
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה explains that the phrase means he pays in whatever metal he named.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: if he specified silver, he gives silver; if he specified gold, he gives gold.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers the question. The metal depends on what the person said when he made the pledge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words of the pledge decide how he pays. If he said silver, it's silver, and if he said gold, it's gold.

keyTerms.meaning: He specified, he said it clearly
Silver
Gold

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
If he specified silver, he gives silver;
if he specified gold, he gives gold.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The metal follows what the person specified in his pledge.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges that רב יהודה's explanation is too obvious to need saying.
steps.simpleTranslation: That's obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא objects that of course you pay what you promised. Why would the משנה need to teach that?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that every line of a משנה teaches something new. If the meaning is plain, the גמרא asks what we are actually learning.

keyTerms.meaning: "That's obvious!": a challenge that a statement teaches nothing new

phrases.english: That's obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב יהודה's explanation as obvious.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's explanation of the משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Paying what you specified needs no teaching.

steps.title: The real lesson: without specifying, anything works
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the lesson is the flip side: if he did not specify, he can pay with any material.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what it teaches us: the reason he must pay silver or gold is that he specified it. But if he didn't specify, he can free himself with anything at all.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the new lesson is hidden in the opposite case. If someone did not name a metal, he can pay his weight in any material.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only requires silver or gold when the person named it. So a plain 'my weight is upon me' can be paid in any material, even cheap ones. The next steps show exactly how far this goes.

keyTerms.meaning: "It teaches us": tells us the new lesson of a statement
The reason: the rule only applies because of this detail
He exempts himself, he fulfills his obligation
With anything at all

steps.whatToRemember: A weight pledge that does not name a metal can be paid in any material.

phrases.english: This is what it teaches us:
the reason is that he specified;
but if he did not specify,
he exempts himself with anything at all.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן: טַעְמָא דְּפֵירַשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge by showing the inference from the opposite case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The phrase only teaches the obvious point that you pay what you named.
steps.terutzMaskana: The phrase teaches that without specifying, any material is acceptable.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the rulings of רחבה and רב פפא, which show how cheap the material can be.

steps.title: רחבה: even pitch counts where it is sold by weight
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא connects this to רחבה, who rules that where pitch is sold by weight, one may pay his weight in pitch.
steps.simpleTranslation: This matches רחבה, who said: in a place where people weigh pitch, he can free himself even with pitch.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רחבה's ruling to show how far 'anything' goes. Even pitch is fine if people there sell it by weight.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a condition: the material must be something people usually sell by weight in that place. Then a weight pledge can be paid with it, even if it is very cheap.

keyTerms.meaning: In a place, in a location
They weigh (when selling)
Pitch, tar

phrases.english: Like Rachava, as Rachava said:
In a place where they weigh pitch,
he exempts himself even with pitch.
phrases.notes: He means someone who pledged his weight without naming a metal. He can pay his weight in pitch.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows a ruling that fits the inference of step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Where pitch is sold by weight, a weight pledge may be paid in pitch.

steps.title: Isn't רחבה's ruling obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges that רחבה's ruling already follows from the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: That's obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רחבה needed to say this. The משנה already implies that any material is fine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'anything' is acceptable, pitch sold by weight is clearly included. So רחבה seems to add nothing.

phrases.english: That's obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רחבה's ruling as obvious.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It already follows from the inference that anything is acceptable.

steps.title: Needed where some weigh pitch and some measure it
steps.stepSummary: רחבה's ruling is needed for a place where some sellers weigh pitch and others measure it by volume.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where some weigh and some measure. You might have said: since not everyone weighs it, no. So it teaches us that it still counts.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that רחבה is talking about a mixed market. Some sellers weigh pitch and others measure it by volume.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think pitch only counts if everyone sells it by weight. רחבה teaches that it is enough if some sellers there weigh it.

keyTerms.meaning: "It is only needed for...": points to a special case where the ruling is new
He measures (by volume)
"You might have said": brings the mistaken assumption the ruling corrects
Since all of them...

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where there are some who weigh and some who measure.
You might have said:
since not all of them weigh it, no, it doesn't count;
so it teaches us that it does.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּאִיכָּא דִּתְקֵל וְאִיכָּא דְּכָיֵיל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge by limiting רחבה to a mixed market.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If not all sellers weigh pitch, it does not count as a weighed item.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even if only some sellers weigh it, pitch counts.

steps.title: רב פפא: even onions count where they are sold by weight
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא rules that where onions are sold by weight, one may pay his weight in onions.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: in a place where people weigh onions, he can free himself even with onions.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא adds another cheap material, onions, to the same rule. It works if they are sold by weight there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This follows the same pattern as רחבה. What matters is that the material is sold by weight locally, not how valuable it is.

keyTerms.meaning: Onions

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
In a place where they weigh onions,
he exempts himself even with onions.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: בְּאַתְרָא דְּתִקְלֵי שַׁמְכֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel ruling to רחבה's, about onions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Where onions are sold by weight, a weight pledge may be paid in onions.

steps.title: Isn't רב פפא's ruling obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא again challenges that the ruling adds nothing new.
steps.simpleTranslation: That's obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: Just as with רחבה, the גמרא asks why רב פפא needed to say this at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Onions sold by weight should clearly count under the rule already taught. So what is רב פפא adding?

phrases.english: That's obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's ruling as obvious.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It already follows from the rule that anything sold by weight is acceptable.

steps.title: Needed where sellers toss in extra onions after weighing
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא's ruling is needed where sellers add two or three free onions after weighing. Even so, it still counts as selling by weight.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where, after they weigh, they throw in two or three more. You might have said the weighing doesn't really count anymore, so it teaches us that it still does.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that רב פפא is talking about a market where sellers add a few free onions after weighing. Even so, onions there still count as sold by weight.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra free onions might make it seem like the weighing is not exact or serious. רב פפא teaches that the item is still a weighed item, so it can be used to pay a weight pledge.

keyTerms.meaning: After
They throw (in)
Two or three
Cancelled, no longer counts
The status of being sold by weight

steps.whatToRemember: A weight pledge without a named metal can be paid in any material sold by weight in that place. This holds even if only some sellers weigh it (pitch), and even if sellers add a few extra after weighing (onions).

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where, after they weigh, they throw in two or three more.
phrases.notes: The seller adds two or three free onions to the buyer's pile after weighing.

phrases.english: You might have said:
the status of being weighed is cancelled;
so it teaches us that it is not.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּבָתַר דְּשָׁקְלִי שָׁדוּ תְּרֵי תְּלָתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge by limiting רב פפא to a market that adds extra onions.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Adding free onions after weighing cancels their status as a weighed item.
steps.terutzMaskana: They still count as a weighed item, so they may be used to pay.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Any material sold by weight locally may be used to pay a weight pledge that did not name a metal.

steps.title: Why does the story contradict the משנה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the story in the משנה about the mother of ירמטיא and asks how a story can contradict the rule it is supposed to illustrate.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'There was a story with the mother of ירמטיא, etc.' The גמרא asks: a story that goes against the rule?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה and points out that the story seems to clash with the rule the משנה just taught.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה taught that if a person vows his weight, he pays in silver only if he said silver, and in gold only if he said gold. In the story, the mother of ירמטיא did not say gold, yet she gave gold. A story is supposed to support the rule, but this one seems to break it.

keyTerms.meaning: A story or real event brought to show how a law works
A story that contradicts the rule, which is a sign that something is off
'Etc.' The quote goes on, but only the opening words are cited

phrases.english: There was an incident with the mother of Yirmatya, etc.
phrases.notes: This is a quote from our משנה. The full story is spelled out in the next step.

phrases.english: An incident to contradict?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from רב פפא's onion ruling to the next line of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The way the משנה places the story right after its rule about paying one's weight in silver or gold.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The rule says you pay gold only if you said gold. In the story she gave gold without saying so. A story should support the rule, not contradict it.

steps.title: An important person pays according to his status
steps.stepSummary: The משנה is missing a line: an important person who did not specify is judged by his status. That is why the mother of ירמטיא gave her daughter's weight in gold.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה is missing words, and this is what it means to teach: if the person is important, then even if he did not say silver or gold, we judge his vow by his status. And that is the story of the mother of ירמטיא. She said, 'My daughter's weight is on me,' and she went up to ירושלים. They weighed her daughter, and she gave her weight in gold.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the problem by saying the משנה left out a line. Once that line is added, the story fits perfectly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The basic rule still holds for an ordinary person: without saying gold, he does not have to give gold. The added line says a wealthy, important person's words are understood by his status. The mother of ירמטיא was such a person, so her vow meant gold.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is missing words.' The משנה left out a line that we must fill in
An important, distinguished (here: wealthy) person
Specified clearly
According to his status or dignity

steps.whatToRemember: An ordinary person's vow is read by its plain words. An important person's vow that leaves out the details is read by his status.

phrases.english: It is missing words
phrases.notes: The גמרא is saying the משנה skipped a line, and it is about to fill that line in.

phrases.english: and this is what it teaches:
And if he is an important person,
even though he did not specify,
we say it is according to his status.
And there was an incident with the mother of Yirmatya
who said, "My daughter's weight is upon me,"
and she went up to Jerusalem, and they weighed her,
and she gave her weight in gold.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 19 by adding a missing line to the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Filling in a missing clause in the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The story seemed to break the rule that gold is owed only if gold was said.
steps.terutzMaskana: For an important person, a vow without details is judged by his status. So the story illustrates the added line and does not contradict the rule.

steps.title: 'My height' versus 'my full height'
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה rules that a vow of 'my height' requires a stiff rod as tall as the person, while 'my full height' can be paid with a bendable rod.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: Someone who says, 'My height is on me,' gives a rod that does not bend, as tall as he is. Someone who says, 'My full height is on me,' gives a rod that does bend.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה gives a new ruling about a person who vows to donate his 'height' instead of his weight.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה treats the two wordings differently. Plain 'my height' means a solid rod that stands straight. Adding the word 'full' (מלא) lets him give even a thin rod that bends, as long as it is as long as he is.

keyTerms.meaning: My height
A rod or staff
Bends; a thin rod that bends over
Full

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
One who says, "My height is upon me,"
gives a rod that does not bend.
"My full height is upon me":
he gives a rod that bends.
phrases.notes: A bending rod is a thin one, so this vow can be paid with less.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: vows of height instead of weight.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'My height' requires a stiff rod as tall as the person. 'My full height' can be paid with a bendable rod of that length.

steps.title: A ברייתא treats both wordings the same
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that both 'my height' and 'my full height' require a rod that does not bend, which goes against רב יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The גמרא challenges him from a ברייתא: 'My height is on me' or 'My full height is on me': in both cases he gives a rod that does not bend.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב יהודה with a ברייתא that sees no difference between the two wordings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה said the word 'full' allows a bendable rod. The ברייתא puts both wordings together and requires a stiff rod for both. So the extra word 'full' seems to change nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: 'My height is on me.' A vow to donate a rod as tall as oneself
'My full height is on me.' The same vow with the extra word 'full'

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
"My height is upon me," or "My full height is upon me":
he gives a rod that does not bend.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב יהודה's ruling from step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's split between 'my height' and 'my full height'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא gives both wordings the same law, a stiff rod. So the word 'full' does not create a new law.

steps.title: רב יהודה follows רבי עקיבא, who learns from extra words
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה's ruling follows the view of רבי עקיבא, who learns meaning from extra words. The ברייתא follows the other view.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said his ruling according to רבי עקיבא, who learns something from extra words.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by saying רב יהודה and the ברייתא follow two different opinions about extra words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא holds that if a person adds a word he did not need, that word must add something. 'Full' is such an extra word, so for רב יהודה it changes the vow. The ברייתא follows those who do not learn from extra words.

keyTerms.meaning: Extra wording; words that were not needed
Reads closely and draws a lesson from it
'He said it according to...' Tying a ruling to one side of a known argument

phrases.english: He said it according to Rabbi Akiva,
who learns from extra language.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא דְּאָמַר כְּרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, דְּדָיֵיק לִישָּׁנָא יַתִּירָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Tying each source to a different תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to prove the word 'full' adds nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: For רבי עקיבא, extra words add meaning, so 'full' allows a bendable rod. The ברייתא follows the opposing view.

steps.title: The source: רבי עקיבא on selling a house with a pit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins quoting a משנה in בבא בתרא to show that רבי עקיבא learns from extra words. The case is a house sale where the pit and cistern are not included.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a משנה: Someone who sells a house has not sold the pit or the cistern, even if he wrote 'its depth and its height.' And the seller has to buy himself a path to reach them. These are the words of רבי עקיבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts bringing its proof that רבי עקיבא learns from extra words. This step is setup: the part where רבי עקיבא actually uses extra words comes in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רבי עקיבא's view, a house sale does not include the pit and cistern. The seller also loses the right to walk through the sold area, so he must buy a path. The proof will come from the next part of this משנה, which shows what happens when the seller adds words he did not need.

keyTerms.meaning: A pit dug in the ground for holding water
A cistern, a water pit built up with walls
'Its depth and its height.' Wording in a sale document
To buy himself a path, a right of way

phrases.english: As we learned in a mishna:
phrases.notes: This משנה is in בבא בתרא, about someone selling a house.

phrases.english: He has sold neither the pit nor the cistern,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁכָּתַב עוֹמְקָהּ וְרוּמַהּ,
phrases.english: even though he wrote "its depth and its height,"
and he must buy himself a path,
phrases.notes: He means the seller, who kept the pit but sold the land around it.

phrases.english: these are the words of Rabbi Akiva.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּתְנַן: לֹא אֶת הַבּוֹר וְלֹא הַדּוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source for the claim in step 23 that רבי עקיבא learns from extra words.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי עקיבא learns meaning from extra words.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in בבא בתרא about selling a house without its pit and cistern. Its proof continues in the following lines.

steps.title: The rest of the house-sale משנה: חכמים argue, and רבי עקיבא agrees in one case
steps.stepSummary: חכמים say the seller does not need to buy a path to his pit, and רבי עקיבא agrees that if the seller said 'except for these,' he does not need a path.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the חכמים say: he does not need to buy a path. And רבי עקיבא agrees that when the seller said to the buyer 'except for these,' he does not need to buy himself a path.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps quoting the משנה from בבא בתרא that it started in the last step. This sets up the proof that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא held that a seller who kept his pit and cistern must buy a path to reach them. Here we learn that even רבי עקיבא agrees there is no need to buy a path if the seller said 'except for these.' That case is the one the גמרא will use as its proof.

keyTerms.meaning: A path. Here it means a way to walk through the sold house to reach the pit and cistern.
'Except for these.' The seller says this when he keeps the pit and cistern for himself.
'And he agrees.' One side admits the other side is right in a certain case.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis say: he does not need to,
phrases.notes: He means the seller does not need to buy a path to reach his pit and cistern.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Akiva agrees
that when he said to him "except for these"
he does not need to buy himself a path.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the quote of the משנה begun in step 24.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי עקיבא learns new meaning from extra words.
steps.raayaSupportSource: משנה in בבא בתרא about selling a house without the pit and cistern.

steps.title: Extra words add meaning, so 'my full height' adds a new rule
steps.stepSummary: Since 'except for these' was not needed but was said, it adds something. In the same way, the extra word 'full' in 'my full height' adds a new rule, which supports רב יהודה as following רבי עקיבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: So we see: since he did not need to say it and he said it anyway, it comes to add something. Here too: since he did not need to say it and he said it anyway, it comes to add something.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the lesson from the משנה and applies it to the vow of 'my full height.' This completes the proof for the answer in step 23.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pit and cistern were not part of the sale anyway, so saying 'except for these' was extra. רבי עקיבא learns from those extra words that the seller also kept a path to them for himself, so he does not need to buy one. The same thinking says the extra word 'full' in 'my full height' must teach something, which is why רב יהודה treats it differently from plain 'my height.'

keyTerms.meaning: 'So we see' or 'evidently.' It introduces a lesson drawn from a source.
'It comes to add something.' The extra words teach a new point.
'Here too.' The same logic is applied to the case being discussed.

steps.whatToRemember: For רבי עקיבא, words that were not needed are never wasted. They add meaning. That is why רב יהודה, following רבי עקיבא, treats 'my full height' differently from 'my height,' while the ברייתא follows חכמים.
steps.whyThisMatters: This closes the challenge from step 22. רב יהודה and the ברייתא simply follow two sides of a known argument about extra words.

phrases.english: Evidently, since he did not need to say it, yet he said it,
phrases.notes: The pit and cistern were not sold anyway, so saying 'except for these' was extra.

phrases.english: it comes to add something,

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא נָמֵי, כֵּיוָן דְּלָא צְרִיךְ וְקָאָמַר
phrases.english: here too, since he did not need to say it, yet he said it,
phrases.notes: This goes back to the vow of 'my full height.' The word 'full' is the extra word.

phrases.english: it comes to add something.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the lesson from the משנה quoted in steps 24-25 and applies it to רב יהודה's ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי עקיבא learns from extra words. רב יהודה follows him in treating 'my full height' differently from 'my height.'

steps.title: New question: what is the law for a vow of 'עומדי'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what someone must give if he vowed 'עומדי' (my standing height).
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: if someone says 'עומדי' (my standing height), what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question about a different wording of the vow. The discussion of this question continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We already know the rules for 'my height' and 'my full height.' Now the גמרא asks about a third wording, 'עומדי,' and wants to know how to measure it.

keyTerms.meaning: 'A question was asked of them.' This opens a real question that the חכמים were unsure about.
Literally 'my standing.' Here it means a vow based on one's standing height or stature.
'What is it?' It asks what the law is.

phrases.english: A dilemma was raised before them:
if one says "my stature," what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After settling 'my height' versus 'my full height,' the גמרא asks about a new wording.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How to measure a vow of 'עומדי,' and whether it is treated like 'my height' or in some other way.
